Hormuz Is Turning Shipping’s Fuel Bill Into a Supply Crisis
The Hormuz crisis is tightening global bunker fuel supplies, with disrupted Middle Eastern and Russian exports driving shortages and longer delivery times.
Soaring marine fuel prices are squeezing shipowners, increasing voyage costs, working capital requirements, and pressure on profit margins.
Global shipping faces growing disruption, as unreliable refueling, limited inventories, and tighter credit threaten trade routes and vessel schedules.
The Hormuz crisis is not only hitting crude oil and gas, but also container shipping. It is also tightening its grip on global shipping through the fuel tanks of vessels carrying world trade. Disrupted exports, constrained refinery supplies, and increasingly unreliable deliveries are clearly at present pushing the bunker market into a dangerous position. Fuel remains available internationally, but securing the right grade at the right port within a commercially workable window is becoming harder. The consequences will be severe, especially for shipowners, as it extends beyond expensive bunkers. Delayed deliveries and uncertain replenishment are not only threatening voyage schedules but also working capital and the profitability of entire trading routes.
This pressure is measurable. On October 16, Vitol estimated that high-sulfur fuel oil flows through Hormuz, including Iranian supplies, remained at least 800,000 tons per month below February levels. At the same time, the successful attacks by Ukraine on Russian refineries have removed an additional estimated million tons monthly. Meanwhile, North Asian refiners were drawing more than a million tons of HSFO for November processing. Global shipping is therefore competing for a constrained product pool. This is a growing reality, even though low-sulfur supplies have received some support from increased exports from China and Nigeria.
Related: German Power Supply Startups Exit Market as Wholesale Prices Soar
These pressures are now converging on a market that depends as much on reliable distribution as on aggregate production. A ton of fuel awaiting export, committed to another customer or stranded behind a disrupted shipping route cannot satisfy an immediate bunker requirement. The market still doesn't seem to recognize this fully. Refinery output, export capacity, blending components, storage and barge availability must all align before a vessel can refuel. Hormuz has weakened several of those links at once, allowing disruption in one location to ripple through the wider supply chain. The spreading of conflict in the Middle East, especially in and around the Bab El Mandeb and Saudi Arabia, is only increasing the impact.
Fujairah illustrates both the market’s adaptability and its continuing vulnerability. Reuters reported on October 1 that third-quarter fuel oil imports had recovered to 2.6 million tons from 845,000 tons in the second quarter. Nevertheless, September imports remained approximately half February’s level. Yes, supplies were returning, but through a system still operating well below earlier import volumes. A partial recovery in cargo movements cannot establish dependable bunker availability when replenishment remains exposed to renewed interruption. The current security situation in and around Hormuz and the Gulf of Oman doesn’t bode well.
The latest delivery assessments show how uneven that recovery remains. ENGINE’s October 13 outlook put Singapore’s recommended very-low-sulfur fuel oil lead times at 11–18 days, compared with 10–15 days a week earlier. HSFO required 11–17 days. Fujairah’s VLSFO availability had improved, while HSFO and low-sulfur marine gasoil remained limited. Key Omani ports offered a more comfortable marine gasoil position, with one supplier quoting one to two days. The emerging crisis is geographically fragmented, with pressure varying by fuel grade and delivery location.
That fragmentation complicates procurement, without making the commercial damage less serious. A ship requiring fuel within three days cannot necessarily absorb a two-week booking window. Physical shortages become commercially disruptive well before a port exhausts its stocks. The critical threshold will be crossed when available supply can no longer accommodate the schedules on which shipping contracts depend.
Inventory figures can consequently offer misleading reassurance. ENGINE reported that Fujairah’s heavy distillate and residual stocks averaged 4.72 million barrels in early October, approximately 5% above September’s average. At the same time, local bunker availability remains severely constrained. Those inventories do not all represent uncommitted, immediately deliverable marine fuel. Product specifications, ownership, and export obligations determine how much can actually reach a vessel. More barrels in storage can coexist with fewer practical purchasing options for an owner facing a departure deadline.
Here, the market and market participants play a pivotal role. The economics of holding inventory add another vulnerability. S&P Global reported in September that strong backwardation, with prompt fuel priced above later deliveries, was discouraging blenders from maintaining stocks. Blending closer to delivery reduced their exposure to falling prices. However, it also increases sensitivity to delayed or unsuitable components. Across a stressed market, individually rational decisions can remove the collective buffer needed to absorb disruption. We are now looking at a situation in which a replenishment delay that would previously have been manageable can then translate directly into a failed delivery.
At the same time, shippers are looking at financial constraints too. Higher prices are already imposing a substantial financing burden. General Index assessed September VLSFO averages at $872 per ton in Singapore and $939 in Fujairah, up 6% and 15.9%, respectively, from August. An additional $100 per ton increases the cost of a 2,000-ton purchase by $200,000, before accounting for waiting time or diversion expenses. Shippers will calculate all of this; if it repeats across a fleet, such increases demand considerably more cash to maintain existing operations. It seems the media still doesn’t understand that even strong headline freight earnings don't automatically translate into stronger margins.
The next constraint could emerge through credit. When fuel prices rise, an unchanged financing facility buys fewer tons. Suppliers need additional funding to maintain throughput, while owners need more liquidity to cover each voyage. If lenders or counterparties tighten terms, physical availability may be accompanied by financial exclusion: fuel can be purchased, but only by buyers able to provide sufficient cash or security. Smaller operators would be particularly vulnerable to this combination of expensive deliveries and reduced purchasing flexibility.
Owners are already adjusting. Reuters reported on October 16 that bunker purchases were becoming smaller and more frequent, with shorter contractual commitments and greater use of alternative locations, including Port Louis, Colombo, and Salalah. This not only helps operators manage immediate exposure but also shifts demand toward ports that must secure additional replenishment and delivery capacity. Geographic diversification improves options; its effectiveness still depends on the fuel and infrastructure available behind each alternative call.
Over the coming weeks, regional shortages will recur, premiums will remain volatile, and booking requirements will lengthen. A broader crisis will occur if additional export losses coincide with refinery outages and reduced tanker availability.
Shipping does not need every bunker hub to run dry for the damage to become systemic. Schedules will be disrupted if persistent uncertainty over delivery remains in place. Hormuz is steadily turning dependable refueling into a more expensive and conditional service. Customers far beyond the Gulf will be feeling the consequences.

items.title: EU tariffs aimed at China hitting Ukraine, steel boss says
items.summary: The boss of one of Ukraine's biggest steel companies says the country has been "bundled together" in measures aimed at curbing cheap imports.
items.content:
By Michael Race ,Â  Business reporter Â  and Â  Simon Jack ,Â  Business editor
The boss of one of Ukraine's biggest steel companies has called on the European Union to drop import restrictions on products made from the country, arguing it has been "bundled together" in measures aimed a curbing cheap imports from the likes of China.
Yuriy Ryzhenkov, chief executive of Metinvest, told the BBC the recently-imposed tariffs on imported steel to the EU were "unfair" and had been put in place "without any consideration for the situation Ukraine is in".
He said he wished to see "at least a carve out" for Ukraine to access the EU market.
A spokesperson for the European Commission said the EU "took into account the difficult situation" of Ukraine when deciding its steel policy.
The trading bloc has recently imposed restrictions on steel imports in an effort to protect steel manufacturers of member nations.
It has capped the amount of steel which can enter the EU tax free at 18.3 million tonnes per year - a 47% reduction from 2024 levels.
There are some country-specific quotas in the policy, but the overall aim is to cut the amount of steel that can be imported due to member nations struggling to compete with cheap imports from the likes of China and Turkey.
Despite a free-trade agreement (FTA) being in place between the EU and Ukraine, the FTA does not stop the EU from introducing separate trade protection measures.
"Ukraine has been bundled together into those measures without any consideration for the situation Ukraine is in," Ryzhenkov said, pointing to the war with Russia.
"Access to the European market is crucial for survival," he added. "The restrictive measures that have been put in place by the authorities in the European Union, they don't help.
"I think it's unfair that Ukraine has been treated in the same way as all of the other importers into the European Union."
The Ukraine steel industry estimates steel exports to the EU could ultimately fall by about 50â60%.
The EU said Ukraine's specific steel quota guaranteed exports of the metal, but acknowledged this was at a "level lower than in the past years".
"Despite the war effort, Ukraine remains an important exporter of steel to the EU," a spokesperson said, adding it had "offered compensations" to its largest suppliers, which included Ukraine.
Image caption, Yuriy Ryzhenkov, chief executive of Metinvest, says EU steel quotas are "unfair" on Ukraine
Steel products are a foundation in Ukraine's economy. Before the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, metallurgy and mining accounted for roughly 10% of Ukraine's national income and a third of its exports. The EU is its top customer.
But the industry has suffered from the continued Russian bombardment.
All of Ukraine's steel mills have been bombed at points since the conflict began in 2022, but Ryzhenkov said strikes had "intensified significantly recently".
At one point in September, there was "no single tonne of steel produced" in Ukraine for the first time in about 150 years, he added.
Almost 800 Metinvest workers have been killed since the war began.
Ryzhenkov said the company had "improved the covered areas" at its mills where workers can shelter during air raids.
"The only thing we can do is to design procedures to keep people safe and just obey those procedures and try to minimise the risks."
"Unfortunately, you cannot cover a whole steel mill to avoid it being damaged."
Ryzhenkov said he expected the coming winter to be "one of the hardest in our history".
"We are in a dire situation when we don't have logistics to access any other market apart from the EU and cutting our available market by 60%, that doesn't help for the industry to survive."

items.title: European diplomats attacked by Israeli settlers in West Bank
items.summary: The Israeli military condemns the violence but the prime minister's office says it is part of a "smear" campaign.
items.content:
Image caption, Masked settlers are accused of attacking the convoy
Diplomatic correspondent ,Â  Reporting from Jerusalem
A delegation of European diplomats has been attacked by masked Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank.
Belgium condemned the assault on its consul general and the other envoys, while France decried the attack as "appalling". Both called for Israel to bring those responsible to justice.
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) also condemned what they called "the severe act of violence" and said they were investigating.
But the office of the Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu cast doubt on what happened, suggesting it was part of a "co-ordinated campaign to smear Israel".
The attack came only a day after a number of Palestinians and Heidi Levine, a Washington Post photographer, were injured in a separate assault by settlers in another village in the West Bank.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the attack on Levine was "disturbing" and "not a good look".
It was also condemned by the US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, who called it a "despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards". A staunch ally of Israel, Huckabee said the assailants must face "prosecution to the fullest extent of the law".
Figure caption, Rubio 'very disturbed' over video of West Bank settler attack on US journalist
In Saturday's incident, the European diplomats - from Belgium, France, Poland and the Catholic Church - had come to the largely Christian village of Taybeh near Ramallah.
They were there to assess the situation on the ground after almost near daily attacks by Israeli settlers on Palestinians trying to bring in their olive harvest.
Video footage from the scene showed masked settlers confronting the convoy. Reports suggest stones were thrown.
The Belgian authorities said a car from its consulate had a window smashed and a French mayor was assaulted. Video showed a man wearing a French tricolor sash slumped beside a vehicle.
Belgium's foreign minister Maxime Prevot condemned the attack and said Israel had a responsibility to bring those responsible to justice, as well as ensuring the safety of diplomats, journalists and Palestinians.
"Palestinians face this violence every day. Settlers also target journalists reporting on it and diplomats. Harvesting olives, reporting the news or carrying out diplomatic duties should never put anyone at risk of attack," he said.
He also said Belgium will continue to press for EU sanctions against those responsible for the violence.
Image caption, Palestinians have been harvesting olives in the West Bank this week before Israeli settlers attack
France's Foreign Minister Jean-NoÃ«l Barrot echoed those sentiments, calling on Israeli authorities to "urgently halt this criminal violence and guarantee the safety of civilian populations".
Poland's foreign affairs ministry also called for a "firm response" from Israeli authorities and for "an end to the spiral of violence in the West Bank".
The EU condemned the attacks, urged Israel to abide by international and human rights law, and end the expansion of settlements.
A spokesperson said that while they acknowledged some Israeli officials had condemned the attacks, they said they still expect "full accountability as well as effective measures" to stop the continued violence against Palestinians and journalists.
Gideon Sa'ar, Israel's foreign minister, said he strongly condemned the violence by what he called "Israeli rioters". He said the foreign ministry was in contact with the ambassadors of the countries involved.
But he added: "Without detracting from the severity of the incident, it is unfortunate that the visit was not coordinated with the IDF in advance. Such coordination could have helped safeguard the visitors' security."
The IDF said they "strongly condemn the severe act of violence that took place in the area of Taybeh, during which diplomatic representatives were attacked by Israeli rioters."
"According to a preliminary inquiry, no IDF soldiers were present at the scene at the time of the attack," they added.
Image caption, Netanyahu's office named the injured French official as Bernard Baudoux, the left-wing mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries
But Netanyahu's office urged "caution before drawing conclusions" from reports about the attack.
It said the images on social media "do not establish the complete sequence of events or individual responsibility".
A statement continued: "Those circumstances remain under investigation. Israeli police and forensic investigators have launched an investigation to establish the facts and identify those responsible."
It added that "these reports come amid concerns about a coordinated campaign to smear Israel and the Jewish residents of Judea and Samaria during the annual olive harvest, relying on sensational headlines before the full facts emerge".
Netanyahu's office named the injured French official as Bernard Baudoux. The left-wing mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries in northern France told the AFP news agency the attack showed a tolerance by Israel's right-wing government for settler violence.
The mayor said the settlers kicked him and beat him with iron bars, throwing him to the ground.
"It's the gratuitous nature of the violence that stuns me," he said. "They arrived completely enraged."
"The whole world needs to know what's happening there. For me, I'll go back to my country and everything will be fine. Those who continue to suffer the most are those who are here," he said.

Electricity costs put UK steelmakers in worst position in three years against EU rivals
Premium paid over French counterparts has risen to almost £30 a megawatt hour, analysis by lobby group finds
British steelmakers have been pushed further behind European rivals on electricity costs after the US-Israeli war on Iran caused a surge in global gas prices.
The premium paid by the British industry over its French counterpart has risen to almost £30 a megawatt hour (MWh), its highest level in three years, according to analysis by the lobby group UK Steel.
Energy prices have long been one of the main factors businesses cite when asked what is holding back British industry. For Andy Burnham they represent perhaps the biggest obstacle to his goal of “reindustrialising” the UK .
Analysts blame the UK’s high electricity prices on its reliance on gas for power generation, which is crucial for cleaner steelmaking with electric arc furnaces .
The way the market is set up means that the wholesale gas price determines the price of electricity even from other sources that cost much less to produce, such as wind or solar power, and Iran’s closure of the strait of Hormuz in response to Donald Trump’s bombing campaign has caused global gas prices to soar .
Electricity prices in France are mainly determined by its nuclear reactors, while in Germany heavily polluting coal still plays a large role in generation.
Graph showing electricity costs in UK, Germany, France and Canada. Comparisons with European rivals are particularly important for the UK because the EU is often the main market for British manufactured products, including about 75% of exported steel, worth about £3bn.
The gap with France had fallen in the previous three years to reach £18 a MWh last year, although it remains below the £153 reached in 2022 when Russia’s invasion of Ukraine caused a crisis in the global gas market. The gap with Germany this year fell slightly to about £12.
Under Keir Starmer most of the costs added by government policy to heavy industrial businesses’ electricity costs were removed last year. The main option to bring the price down further, however, would be to set up more cheap renewables – a challenge in the short term – or to directly subsidise prices.
The director general of UK Steel, Peter Brennan, said direct subsidies were the only option to help steelmakers. The lobby group has proposed a cap on prices that it estimates would cost about £51m a year. The government would pay the difference when prices go above that level, while the industry would pay the government if prices go below.
“British steelmakers are being asked to compete with one hand tied behind their backs,” Brennan said. “Despite welcome government action, our electricity prices remain vastly higher than those of our European and global competitors, and the gap with France is getting worse.
“The government has rightly made reindustrialisation a national priority. But we cannot rebuild British manufacturing while forcing our steelmakers to pay substantially more for electricity than their competitors.”
Separately, the government announced measures on Monday to support more than 100,000 workforce opportunities in the eight key growth sectors in its industrial strategy. The “jobs plans” are intended to help young people find work, with a focus on professional and business services, the defence sector and construction.
Similar plans for financial services, clean energy and life sciences have already been announced. Plans for advanced manufacturing and the creative industries are expected to follow shortly.
A government spokesperson said: “We are tackling industry’s number one concern head-on by reducing electricity bills by up to 25% for over 10,000 manufacturing businesses, and cutting costs for hundreds of our most electricity-intensive businesses by around £1bn per year – delivering on the prime minister’s pledge to reindustrialise Britain.”

items.content:
Iran’s Revolutionary Guard says oil tanker struck mine and caught fire in Strait of Hormuz
Iran’s Revolutionary Guard says oil tanker struck mine and caught fire in Strait of Hormuz
Iranian force warns of ‘firm response’ against vessels operating with navigation and identification systems switched off
ISTANBUL An oil tanker caught fire after striking a naval mine in the southern part of the Strait of Hormuz, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy said late Sunday.
The blast struck the vessel’s engine room as it attempted to leave the strategic waterway, Iran’s semi-official Fars News Agency reported, citing an IRGC Navy statement.
The tanker had switched off all its positioning and navigation systems from the start of its voyage and attempted to use what Tehran considers an unauthorized southern route, according to the statement.
The IRGC Navy accused the vessel of violating maritime regulations governing passage through the strait.
It warned that ships operating in the Strait of Hormuz and the Gulf with their navigation and identification systems switched off would face a firm response.
The statement did not identify the tanker or provide information on possible casualties or the extent of the damage.
The announcement follows a series of similar incidents in the strategic waterway.
On Saturday, the IRGC Navy said a second supertanker carrying more than 2 million barrels of crude oil struck a naval mine and caught fire while attempting to cross the strait through an unauthorized route.
A day earlier, the Iranian force reported that another tanker had struck a mine, triggering an explosion and fire.
The US and Israel launched a war against Iran on Feb. 28. Tehran responded with missile and drone attacks across the region and effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, while Washington later imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports.
The US and Iran subsequently signed a memorandum of understanding in June concerning freedom of navigation in the strait, but implementation stalled over disagreements related to security in the strategic waterway.

You've no doubt noticed that since the war with Iran broke out, gas prices have spiked: up more than 50% since January. But there's another, less well known, natural resource also impacted by the conflict: helium. The world — and the war — don't function without it. No helium? No new cellphones, laptops, cars, MRI machines, missiles: all require this finite and irreplaceable resource. The closing of the Strait of Hormuz in February trapped one-third of the global helium supply. Then just weeks later: Iranian strikes on Qatar's major gas facility further rattled the supply chain. With the extent of the damage unknown, American industry is left desperate for answers as the helium crisis remains up in the air.
Last march as a new war raged, Iranian missiles and drones hit military targets throughout the Middle East: oil tankers stuck in the Persian Gulf, and energy infrastructure. All of it meant to destabilize the global economy.
One of those high value targets attacked: Ras Laffan in Qatar - the world's largest facility for natural gas – and its byproduct helium. 7,100 miles away at the University of Chicago, Joe Sachleben was watching closely from his lab.
Jon Wertheim: When you heard the news that there was an attack on the facility in Qatar, where did your thoughts go?
Joe Sachleben: Um I hope that people weren't hurt was first. And then second, it's like, this is gonna be a problem. I mean, I won't say the words - I was thinking. But, you know, it's, like, crap. We're gonna have to deal with this and I might not be able to get helium.
Helium is critical for those large cylinders: nuclear magnetic resonance machines. In Sachleben's lab, these machines are used by students, but also for higher stakes research to develop breast cancer drugs, immunotherapies, and treatments for Alzheimer's. Suddenly, it's all imperiled, collateral damage from the Iran war.
Helium is the coldest liquid on earth. So every couple months, Sachleben uses this long tube to pour 100 liters of helium on these magnets to stabilize them at 452 degrees below zero Fahrenheit.
Joe Sachleben: Once it gets to a critical level, we have to put helium back in the magnet to keep it cold.
Joe Sachleben: If that doesn't happen, w-- we break the magnet.
Jon Wertheim: You-- you've got problems if that doesn't--
Jon Wertheim: You're saying there-- there's no workaround here. There-- there's no other substance you can substitute in?
Sachleben's lab contracts with one supplier to deliver the helium he needs each month. First U of Chicago's supplier placed Sachleben and his colleagues on what's called "allocation," essentially rationing.
Joe Sachleben: They basically have said, "Well, we'll give you 50% of what you used last year." That doesn't help us. And so what we have to do is decide which machine are we going to sacrifice and which one are we gonna try to keep.
Joe Sachleben: That's where we are now if we can't get the helium.
Joe Sachleben: Fortunately, we found another supplier that is giving us helium on a fairly regular basis. But they can't guarantee it. So we never know if they're gonna say, "Oh, this week, we don't have any."
Then last month, Sachleben got a message saying that supplier was about to run out.
It's not just university research labs. One fifth of the world's helium is consumed by the semiconductor industry alone to make every modern day electronic you might use, from your iPhone to your pacemaker.
Outside Minneapolis, we visited one of those chip makers, Polar Semiconductors.
Surya Iyer: Alright so go ahead and put that on first.
We suited up alongside Surya Iyer, Polar's president and COO, to go inside what's called the "Fab", the ultra sterilized area where they make the chips.
Our barriers to entry so to speak: two masks, two booties, and two pairs of gloves.
Jon Wertheim: You wonderhow-- how many people going to the Mall of Americas have no idea what's going on a few hundred yards away.
Inside, workers in round-the-clock shifts manufacture semiconductors for engine systems in cars, the U.S. military, and those ubiquitous data centers around the country.
Surya Iyer: I would say almost 40%, 50% of the machines in this factory would have helium in some way or the other in the machine.
Jon Wertheim: So it's not just one step of the process.
Surya Iyer: No, no, no. Hundreds of steps in the process involve helium.
Such as this machine, where helium keeps the environment clean and stable to avoid defects on the wafers.
Polar is able to hedge its helium reserves by relying on three suppliers. Still, the company has felt the effects of the shortage. One of their suppliers has put them on allocation as well - that rationing program.
Jon Wertheim: Just to be clear, if you did not have helium, what would happen in this facility?
Surya Iyer: Well, that's a situation that I don't want to even imagine,because if we do not have helium, we'll have to shut down. And–
And the helium crisis is hitting at a time when Polar Semiconductors plans on doubling production capacity to 140 million chips a month.
Surya Iyer: Demand is not going down. The AI data centers are growing lot of demand for semiconductors. Electrification is growing demand for semiconductors. And that means the demand for helium is gonna be growing for a long time.
Jon Wertheim: These data centers we keep hearing about, trillions of dollars popping up all over the U.S. Those don't happen if we don't have helium.
Surya Iyer: Oh, yeah. Without helium, none of these things happen. That's why local supply, supply in the United States is so important to us.
Besides Qatar, the United States is the other major producer of helium for the world. And most of that comes from a single facility in Wyoming. U.S. helium exports are up 70% since the war began and Ras Laffan was hit. This is mostly to accommodate countries manufacturing semiconductors. But the U.S. can't offset the shortage indefinitely.
And here's another issue: ramping up production of helium is not easy, even if you can find it. Four hours north of the Twin Cities we visited the site of a helium discovery, the Topaz Project. Cliff Cain is president of the startup exploration company.
Cliff Cain: So this is a wellhead. We drill down around 3,500 feet. We hit the pocket of gas down there, and -- up comes the gas. It will come out this gauge here. And-- that's how it goes.
And once it goes, this finite resource is gone forever.
For the record, Cain estimates about a dollar of helium is released every second that valve is open. His company has inserted seven wells around a 100-square-mile plot of land.
In most cases — including the Qatar facility — helium is a byproduct of the money-maker: natural gas extraction. In Minnesota, though, it's all helium, all the time. But finding helium is one thing. Getting it to market, even in the best case scenario, will take years.
Jon Wertheim: This is all encouraging. But this isn't gonna help us next month.
Cliff Cain: It's not gonna help us next month. It's not easy to find. It's not easy to build. The logistics are hard, right? You've gotta keep-- something that's 452 degrees below zero cold. And it's perishable.
That's because helium starts to boil off as soon as it's in transit. It's that complicated supply chain that worries Cain, making helium, he says, particularly vulnerable to disruption.
Cliff Cain: We've been trying to warn the markets about this for decades. We're too concentrated with our supply in the world. When you look at it, you've got supply in Qatar. You have some supply in Algeria. You have a little in Poland. You have a source in Russia. And we have a few here in the United States. So all it takes is a few of those to fall and the whole supply chain comes unraveled.
The longer the war with Iran continues, the tighter the global supply of helium gets. But how tight? That's difficult to answer. If helium is hard to acquire, so is information about it.
Rich Brooke: Oh, yes. Absolutely. It's a very tight-knit-- business with these six main players who are-- responsible for the majority of the sales.
Rich Brooke would know. He's a former executive at Air Liquide, one of the six major international helium suppliers, and is now an industry consultant.
Jon Wertheim: How much have prices gone up this year?
Rich Brooke: The spot market prices have tripled. And-- and they can go even higher because--
Jon Wertheim: --expensive to fill your car up with gas.
Jon Wertheim: The U.S. produces helium as well. Are there countries that had been relying on Qatar that are now coming to the U.S. for their supply?
Rich Brooke: Yes. Absolutely. Especially the countries that were-- heavily-- requiring helium for their semiconductor industries, there's only been traditionally two qualified sources. Qatar and Exxon, which is here in the U.S. When Qatar went down, those companies, which are predominantly based in places like Korea and Taiwan and Singapore, immediately started looking-- towards the U.S. for supplies.
Jon Wertheim: How long can the U.S. accommodate this demand from other countries?
Rich Brooke: Well, it depends on how long the shortage lasts. And also it depends on-- on how much product we can continue to recover out of the-- out of the caverns.
He's referring to helium storage caverns — two in the U.S., one in Germany — illustrated in this diagram in blue. They are underground, made of salt, and naturally impermeable, which makes them ideal for holding excess helium when the market is long.
Jon Wertheim: Do we have any idea how much helium is in these caverns?
Rich Brooke: So that's a closely held secret by the-- owners of the cavern. The market at one point last year was long. So they were actually taking helium and pumping it into those caverns. Of course, now they've reversed the direction.
Jon Wertheim: Three months from now, what does supply look like?
Rich Brooke: Well, if you can tell me what's gonna happen in the Strait of Hormuz between now and three months from now, I can tell you exactly what'll be happening in the helium business. Unfortunately, you can't and so I can't.
In the aftermath of the Iranian strikes on Ras Laffan in March, the Qataris said it would take at least three years to get the facility back in full operation. We wanted to know about the extent of the damage of the helium infrastructure specifically, but our requests for comment went unanswered.
With so much at stake — and so much swirling uncertainty about the state of this vital element — we enlisted Joe Bermudez to assess how bad it could get. A senior imagery analyst at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, Bermudez looked for clues using what little information we do have. It comes from a satellite…
Joe Bermudez: It'd be nice if the Qatari government-- shared a little more…
We provided Bermudez two images of an area of Ras Laffan that facilitates helium production - one before the Iranian strikes in March; one four days after.
He showed us this area where he says that it looks like water or firefighting foam dried to make a black stain on the cement.
Joe Bermudez: It looks like-- something necessitated the pipes in this area, the equipment in this area to be hosed down.
Jon Wertheim: So you're not prepared to say what it was or the severity, but something happened?
For all the unanswered questions about the extent of the damage at the Qatar facility, this we know: the helium supply chain issues are sufficiently serious that Cliff Cain has briefed policymakers in Washington.
Jon Wertheim: When you addressed the Pentagon about helium, specifically, what were you telling them?
Cliff Cain: That we have a problem. We have a single, critical point of failure in the system. We have Qatar go down. Now that single, critical point of failure is coming closer to term. And I think that's what's got us concerned, it's 'cause that's all it does take.
Cain says it's especially concerning given that on account of the war with Iran, the U.S. is experiencing a munitions shortage — and yet the Pentagon has asked some defense contractors to quadruple their production capacities of certain weapons.
Cliff Cain: You can't make modern warfare without helium. And that's just a fact. You've heard about the missiles, the hypersonics. Without helium, you can't make the fiber optics. You can't produce the munitions. You can't produce the electronics that goes on these things. And so if you don't have helium, your opportunity to make war becomes even more difficult.
We are seven months into the war now, with no end in sight. Since September, nearly two dozen ships have been hit while attempting to pass through the Strait of Hormuz. And no ships carrying helium are leaving Qatar.
Produced by Lucy Hatcher. Associate producer, Jessica Kegu. Broadcast associate, Mimi Lamarre. News associate, Eric Frank. Edited by Michael Mongulla.

items.title: Inside the shadowy world of anti-Putin sabotage from within Russia
items.summary: Two men tell of the work they say they have been doing to support Ukrainian intelligence during the war.
items.content:
Figure caption, Watch: Russian saboteur working for Ukraine shares reconnaissance videos
Two Russian men secretly working for Ukraine's intelligence services have given rare accounts of operations they claim to have been involved with, that have targeted military assets and personnel inside Russia.
One of the men, whom we are calling Ivan, claims to have played a role from Russia in Ukrainian drone attacks on strategic bombers and munitions factories on his home soil.
He features in a BBC World Service documentary about the shadowy world of Russian saboteurs.
The documentary, by independent Polish journalist Marcin Mamon, also features a man we are calling Foma, a Russian living in exile in Poland.
Foma runs a network of undercover volunteers in Russia, that surveils high-level officers that the GUR - Ukraine's military intelligence service - is considering targeting, he says. He stresses they are never involved in the attacks themselves.
He was also tight-lipped about who they were surveilling, but after Lt Gen Fanil Sarvarov was assassinated in December last year in Moscow , Foma admitted he had provided the Ukrainians with intelligence on him.
Image caption, Lt Gen Fanil Sarvarov was killed in Moscow last year by an explosive device hidden under his car
There have been previous media reports of Russian sabotage groups, but it is rare to get access to someone operating on the ground, like Ivan, explaining alleged activities.
The GUR has confirmed that Ivan and Foma are both working for the agency. But it also has acknowledged that it cannot know the full picture. When Ivan's handler was pressed on whether he could be trusted, the handler replied: "I'm not sure of anyone, except myself."
And both the GUR and the men are cautious about how much detail they share, making it impossible to verify the activities the men claim to have carried out.
The broad tactics Ivan and Foma describe, however, have been acknowledged by the Ukrainian authorities. Kyiv has spoken of its strategy of co-ordinated drone attacks on what it claims are legitimate targets inside Russia, and has acknowledged it uses secret agents for this.
There have also been several political assassinations in Russia since the start of the war. As a matter of policy, Ukraine never officially admits or claims responsibility for targeted attacks, though a Ukrainian intelligence officer has previously admitted to the BBC it was behind the killing of senior military figure Lt Gen Igor Kirillov in December 2024.
It is difficult to confirm how many Russians are doing this kind of work for Ukraine. According to Foma, they number about 300-500, though this is impossible to verify.
If you are outside the UK, watch on YouTube , external and listen to the BBC World Service Documentary Podcast - Shadowmen: Russians working with Ukraine
Ivan and Foma say they are both opposed not just to Russia's war in Ukraine, but to President Vladimir Putin's regime - and believe his political future depends on the war's outcome.
"At the moment... I think the [Putin] regime might fall if they lose the warâ¦ Through our actions... we are trying to speed this up," Ivan says.
His work, he told Mamon, involved surveilling military sites, and locating places to hide drone components, in preparation for potential attacks on Russian assets.
"When these [drone] components are combinedâ¦ it turns out a formidable weapon, which with a single blow can destroy an object that costs many, many millions of dollars," Ivan said.
He sent Mamon a video which showed him apparently hiding explosives near a Russian military airfield.
If he had been caught, he would have been charged with terrorism, and jailed for decades.
Foma's work is different - he operates remotely, training his volunteers in Russia, online. Mamon watched him conducting one such tutorial - on how to trail a senior military official marked for surveillance.
Image caption, Foma explained how he taught his undercover volunteers to trail Russian officers
"You will get a file... from me or a colleagueâ¦ with the proposed target. The file will contain [the target's] photo, his data, his details, date of birth, age, and a description of him. There'll be information on his car, if he has one. When you go to the target, don't take a phone," he told his volunteers.
Foma was once part of the Russian elite, so he claims to have a unique set of contacts and constant flow of insider information.
He showed Mamon on his laptop how he mapped military targets.
"This shows a database... the location of storage warehouses, and military units. Where generals liveâ¦ Where the pilots of strategic bombers who shell Ukraine live.
"In order to break the system, you need to understand how it works. Then you can aim for their weak points."
He said there were about "three dozen" people in his network split between Russia, Ukraine and elsewhere in Europe, with the contingent outside Russia providing logistical support, such as tracking targets' digital footprints.
Foma stressed that the GUR suggests the targets to be surveilled, but that he and his team check for themselves that these individuals should be considered military criminals.
"As a ruleâ¦ we also check the data [on that person]â¦ Only after that we say whether we work or not."
But he argued that his team's actions were justified.
"I want people who do terrible things on behalf of Putin and Russia in Ukraineâ¦ to understand that they'll have to pay for it. I want them to get scared."
Foma stressed that he only passed on intelligence to the Ukrainians, and his network did not carry out any assassinations themselves.
Of the assassination of Gen Sarvarov, killed in December 2025, he later texted Mamon to say: "Keeping track of him took quite an effort. He lived alternately with his mistress and his colleague. Covered his tracks and constantly changed his schedule."
But Foma did not share any plans with Mamon and the BBC in advance.
Ivan, however, was tight-lipped about the work he had been involved with, even after the event.
After checking with his military intelligence contacts in both Ukraine and Russia, he thought it likely that Ivan had been involved in a plan to strike Russia's largest military drone factory at Yelabuga in June last year , external . One person was reported to have been killed in the incident.
Ivan stressed that the aim is always to try to avoid harming civilians.
"The most serious case was when my car was stopped for inspection and I had the handmade explosives on me. The risk was very high - however as you can see, I was not detected," he said.
To mitigate the risk of being compromised, "there is no clear structure" to the work, he said, adding he had never met and did not know the identity of others he had been working alongside.
"As soon as you start gathering people in groups, in general chatsâ¦ leaving a mark on the internet, with a high probability this whole group will be quickly detained or destroyed," he said.
Ivan stressed there were few people left in Russia suitable for this kind of work.
"Most of the ideological people have either left the country or are already behind bars," he said.
Many Russians involved in sabotage work on their native soil are therefore either oblivious - for example lorry drivers unaware that their cargoes have been compromised - or are individuals who have been paid, the BBC understands.
Ivan, on the other hand, says he is doing this work for ideological reasons - he used to be a member of the political opposition. As such, his movements would be expected to be monitored closely by the Russian authorities.
So it was a surprise that he managed to frequently leave Russia and return.
Image caption, Marcin waiting to meet Ivan in Georgia - we were surprised by Ivan's apparent freedom to travel
Mamon persuaded Ivan to drive him into the Georgian desert, where they could speak freely - and asked him how the Ukrainians could trust him.
"You go to a third countryâ¦ where [Ukraine's] agents meet youâ¦ and conduct lie detector tests," Ivan told him.
Mamon asked Ivan to put him in touch with one of his GUR handlers in Ukraine. This man immediately rang Ivan on speaker phone - apparently demonstrating that Ivan worked for him. They spoke in code, referring to "repairs at the school".
But later, the handler admitted he could not rule out the possibility Ivan might work for the Russians too, either voluntarily or under duress.
Foma thinks the fact that Ivan can travel freely does not necessarily constitute a red flag.
"There are all sorts of holes in [the country's governance], and if you know them, or are just lucky, then you can jump through the holesâ¦ and live in the system. Like a mouse in a piece of cheese," he told Mamon.
Perhaps more compellingly, if Ivan had also been spying for FSB, it would seem likely that he would share what he knew of Ukraine's attack plans with the Russian agency. More than a year before a devastating strike by more than 100 Ukrainian drones, Ivan had been telling Marcin there would be a major attack on strategic bombers on military airfields across Russia, though he never said when or where.
"Fear is always present," he said. "It follows me everywhere. Even if you don't do anything, you're still afraid. This is Russia."
But he was optimistic that eventually his life would change.

items.title: Australian Greens senator denies claims of misconduct towards women
items.summary: Jordon Steele-John says the timing of the claims is motivated by "nasty political games" within the Greens.
items.content:
Image caption, Greens senator Jordon Steele-John denies claims of misconduct against women
An Australian Greens senator has denied allegations of inappropriate behaviour towards women and accused his party of "nasty political games", days after the claims emerged.
Last Thursday, Greens leader David Shoebridge said Senator Jordon Steele-John, 32, had taken leave from the party room after a letter from seven current and former members said he had been accused of "multiple allegations" of misconduct between 2017 and 2025.
In an online post on Sunday, the senator denied the claims and said he was not on leave. On a sexual assault claim, he said police investigating the matter had closed the case and no charges were laid.
An internal party probe has been launched into the allegations.
Steele-John, who has cerebral palsy and uses a wheelchair, was first elected to the senate in Western Australia in November 2017.
In his letter responding to the claims, Steele-John said his nickname - "Feels on wheels" - initially referred to him being emotional when advocating for disability rights but had since taken on a "more sinister meaning" about his alleged mistreatment of women.
He accused Shoebridge of mishandling the matter and questioned the timing of the letter, saying "it is no coincidence" that the allegations were sent to the leader "the day after we agreed on the timeline for the next preselection" ahead of the next federal election.
Days after the letter with the claims was sent to Shoebridge, local media reported that the party had created a 47-page dossier years earlier that listed a number of allegations against Steele-John and how to manage media coverage if they emerged.
Steele-John said the dossier was made so that the media would not "bombard" the two women at the centre of those claims and that neither woman had made a complaint.
He acknowledged the allegations against him would have "damaged" the public's trust in him and said he was "committed to rebuilding that by acting with as much transparency and accountability as I can".
Shoebridge's office confirmed that the allegations had been referred to the Independent Parliamentary Standards Commission.

items.title: Trump says suspension of Russia sanctions is to keep peace negotiations going
items.summary: The US president blocked numerous sanctions on Russia two days before they were due to take effect.
items.content:
US President Donald Trump has said his decision to suspend several Russian sanctions is an effort to keep Moscow at the negotiating table.
"I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine," Trump said on his Truth Social messaging platform, adding that he didn't want to "do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table".
Trump blocked numerous sanctions on Russia on Friday night, two days before they were due to take effect, as a row with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky deepened.
Zelensky told NBC News on Sunday that siding with Russian President Vladimir Putin would be a "historic mistake".
Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev has responded to Trump's order by calling it "an important and truly historic moment". He said the sanctions, which were passed by the US Congress and signed into law by the US president in September, would have inflicted "serious damage" on the US and global market.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has described the suspension of the sanctions as a 60-day pause during which their potential impact on the US and global economies would be analysed.
In his Truth Social post, Trump also said Zelensky "doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did", adding "he could have made a better deal two years ago than he can now".
Zelensky has pushed for an end to fighting, and has repeatedly said that Putin doesn't want peace, since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Relations between Washington and Kyiv frayed after the US struck a controversial deal to import Russian diesel last week.
Despite the international sanctions, Russia has still been able to export oil, much of it to China and India - often at attractive discounts. According to the think-tank Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), China has taken about half of Russia's crude exports, with India accounting for about 37%.
In remarks to a European Union summit, after Trump announced the deal to buy diesel from Russia and said Zelensky was "more difficult to deal with" than Putin, Zelensky said it was nice to be among "real leaders".
Image caption, Ukraine's President Zelensky attended an EU leaders' summit in Brussels on Friday
Zelensky has repeatedly pushed for stringent sanctions to limit funding that Russia can use in its war effort. After the latest move from the US, however, he said he believed the Trump administration would lift more sanctions against Russia.
Ukraine and its European allies criticised Trump's plans to import Russian diesel to help lower US energy prices, which have skyrocketed during the Iran war.
The deal, according to Zelensky, was tantamount to the US investing in Russia's war effort.
Concerns that Trump is siding with Russia have been heightened by disruption to Starlink, a US-provided satellite system used by Ukraine. That hampered Kyiv's ability to protect itself from Russian attacks.
Zelensky said US officials had linked speed restrictions to technical issues.
However, he said Ukraine had tested Starlink on EU territory and found it was operating at higher speeds.
Trump has denied both deliberately slowing down the network and a further accusation from Zelensky that the US had stopped sharing defence intelligence.

It’s approaching 5pm in Paris, as we await French President Emmanuel Macron’s televised response to large-scale protests and unrest across France on Saturday.
Macron will address the French public on TV at 8pm (7pm BST) after crisis meetings with ministers on Sunday.
France’s interior minister Laurent Nunez said “the Republic will not yield” after 1,800 were arrested across the country on Saturday.
Protests which had begun about education and schooling conditions in France have broadened to wider cost of living issues.
Buildings were set alight, including Limoges City Hall in central France, as other cities suffered widespread vandalism.
More than 500 police officers, gendarmes and firefighters were injured.
Nunez blamed thousands of “far left” protesters along with criminals who “looted and ransacked” buildings.
The numbers of protesters on Saturday have varied, with authorities saying 550,000 took to the streets nationwide, but organisers said it was about 800,000.
Paris police said 110,000 took part in a march. Sunday has not seen similar incidents.
The cost of damage to shops will run to hundreds of millions of euros, according to the president of a trade body.
US president Donald Trump said “France is burning” and blamed immigration in a post on Truth Social.
Other protests took place against the cost of living in Spain, Italy and Portugal.
Our Paris correspondent Angelique Chrisafis has this dispatch from France , ahead of Emmanuel Macron’s address to the nation on Sunday night.
The French government was in crisis talks on Sunday after one of the most violent days of unrest in years left public buildings burned, hundreds of shops destroyed and looted and more than 2000 people arrested in cities across the country.
Politicians on the left and far-right called for the resignation of the interior minister, Laurent Nunez after the government appeared to have been caught by surprise by the scale of violence. State buildings were stormed and torched, bus-stops smashed, roads barricaded and shops broken into and destroyed.
The president Emmanuel Macron , who is standing down next spring as the far-right Marine Le Pen polls high for the presidential election, was preparing to address the nation on Sunday night.
He wrote on social media there was “no place for violence” in France.
Police and officials faced challenges of different types on Saturday.
First, tens of thousands of peaceful protestors attended calm marches through major cities including Paris, supporting schoolchildren’s demands for more teachers and repairs to decrepit schools .
Those marches, which came after four weeks of street marches and barricades of schools , were attended by parents, teachers and grandparents as well as students and workers protesting over the high cost of living.
The demonstrators carried banners saying the government was not listening to them and calling for more money for public services.
But separately to those peaceful demonstrations, different groups caught police and officials by surprise with moving gatherings, sporadic burning, barricading streets and clashing with police in different parts of cities including Paris , Bordeaux, Nice and Marseille.
Finally, masked looters took advantage of what French media called the “chaos” on the streets to smash shopfronts and grab goods.
If you’re just catching up on the demonstrations across Europe which turned violent on Saturday, this is why some of them are happening.
Why are people taking to the streets across Europe?
People have been protesting in countries across Europe, including Spain, France and Portugal over their unhappiness at the state of schools and wider cost of living crisis.
In France , the activism has largely been led by high school pupils who have clashed with police in often violent protests over long hours, missing teachers, dilapidated classrooms and an opaque university admissions system. Pupils routinely miss months of teaching due to unfilled staff absences.
Other demonstrators have then joined student marches to voice their unhappiness about rising living costs, including over fuel prices after US bombing caused the effective closure of the strait of Hormuz.
The General Confederation of Labour (CGT), one of France’s largest unions, has backed the protests and called for lower prices, higher pensions and boosted wages.
French president Emmanual Macron is nearing the end of his time in the Élysée Palace after serving two terms.
Over the Pyrenees in Spain activists took to the streets in September over housing prices.
They were triggered by the eviction of a 87-year-old woman from her home after an investment fund hiked her rent by 230%. María del Carmen Abascal died a fortnight later after being admitted to hospital.
Protesters have called for lower rents, an end to evictions and a ban on investment funds buying property.
Similar pleas were made across the Iberian border in Portugal on Saturday, with hundreds gathering in central Lisbon.
Portuguese housing prices rose by 124% between 2015 and 2024, roughly twice as fast as the EU average, according to official data.
Squeezed household budgets were also at the centre of marches in Milan, Italy .
A march on Saturday began peacefully but ended with masked rioters throwing stones, paving blocks and other objects at riot police and setting fire to barricades made from bar tables.
Meanwhile student-protests in Albania against the prime minister, Edi Rama, entered their sixth day on Sunday.
Demonstrators have said they are unhappy with perceived corruption , a lack of jobs and poor education standards.
The education protests in France began in late September, week after the start of the school year.
However demonstrations have since intensified, reaching the high point on Saturday.
Saturday was also the first day of cost of living protests in Italy, Portugal and Belgium.
In Albania protests have been taking place since the summer, triggered by a luxury coastal development backed by Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner.
In France the government has said it would deploy 3,000 more substitute teachers to deal with shortages, and said it would include students in decision-making for schools.
It also scrapped plans to increase some university registration fees, which it had announced for next year’s budget.
Fuel protests in mid-September led to an announcement by the Elysee that the government would increase petrol subsidies for certain industries.
Spain’s president Pedro Sánchez attempted to pass emergency housing legislation that would have protected tenants in the rental market.
The Socialist party leader’s defeat led him to calling an early election for 29 November , as he told the public he needed a “broader progressive majority” to get the new laws through.
Macron will give a televised address on Sunday night after holding a crisis meeting with key ministers.
His interior minister Laurent Nunez appeared to signal the French government are not willing to concede further, as he blamed “far left” protesters and “criminals who looted and ransacked” buildings across France.
If Sanchez wins the Spanish election in November, and is able to pass the emergency housing legislation that was stymied last month, then it could see marches in Spain end.
The US president Donald Trump said “France is burning” and the country has been “shattered” by immigration in a post on Truth Social.
He said: “France is burning! The immigration of people from an entirely different world, people with hatred in their hearts, has shattered that once-great country. Close your borders and take control before it is too late!”
French authorities and police have not linked immigrants to the rioting and have repeatedly attributed some of the violence to “radical far-left groups” and other people who joined to loot.
Trump’s post comes after similar comments made by vice president JD Vance on Saturday.
“Western liberals imported the third world into France and other countries in the name of diversity and compassion. They ignored fundamental questions of assimilation and compatibility. They were told it would lead to this and they didn’t listen,” Vance wrote on X.
“I pray that France, a beautiful country of amazing people, will stop this madness before more of its landmarks burn,” he added.
Elsewhere in Europe , violent protests are also continuing Albania, where thousands have been calling for the prime minister to step down as they rally against poor university conditions, high tuition fees and corruption.
Albanian’s capital saw protests on Sunday for a sixth day in a row as the prime minister, Edi Rama, ruled out resigning, the main demand of the protesters.
Hundreds of protesters gathered again in Tirana on Sunday at noon in front of the education ministry chanting “Rama, resign” in a tense standoff with the police, who later used water cannons and tear gas to hold back the crowds.
A protester prepares to throw a petrol bomb toward riot police during clashes at an anti-government demonstration in Tirana, Albania. Photograph: Hameraldi Agolli/AP Shops and institutions in the centre of the city have secured their doors and windows with metal shutters, while city workers removed paving stones to prevent their use by protesters.
In an over-an-hour long video broadcast earlier in the day, Rama ruled out resigning, stating that the protests are the “work of an outside hand”.
Writer and activist Lura Elezi, 38, told AFP that she is protesting for “a better life, rule of law and against crime and corruption”.
“I love my country, but my government does not respect us - it defies us. Every citizen must take responsibility for their country, taking on the duty to lead, to love, and not to destroy one’s own nation,” she said.
Tirana saw its harshest violence on Saturday when protesters threw rocks, Molotov cocktails, metal objects and pyrotechnic devices at police, and torched cars and litter bins, using them as blazing barricades to stop police advancing.
A protester throws a cobblestone during an anti-government demonstration in central Tirana Saturday Photograph: Armend Nimani/AFP/Getty Images The morning newspapers after the night before, here’s how the French press covered Saturday’s protests on Sunday morning.
Le Parisien Dimanche captured the scenes in the Capital with protests taking place near the Monument à la République.
Le Parisien Dimanche on 18 October Photograph: frontpages.com Left leaning newspaper Libération went with “Giving a voice to students”, referring to the genesis of the protests.
Libération on 18 October. Photograph: frontpages.com The financial Sunday newspaper La Tribune Dimanche’s front page was headlined “Six months until the Presidential election: Chaos”, again showing the scenes near the Monument à la République.
La Tribune Dimanche on 18 October Photograph: frontpages.com The centre-right newspaper Le Figaro referred to a “a month of blockades and destruction”.
Le Figaro on 18 October. Photograph: frontpages.com Meanwhile France’s widest-read paid national daily newspaper Le Monde details how Macron “lost the youth”, referring to the protests.
Le Monde on 18 October. Photograph: frontpages.com French President Emmanuel Macron will hold a crisis meeting with ministers on Sunday before he addresses the public, Agence France Presse reports.
Macron will sit down with members of his cabinet on Sunday, the Elysee has said, ahead of his televised speech to the French public this evening.
It was to come as France counts the cost of Saturday’s protests, which saw clashes, arson and widespread looting.
Ministers have blamed “ultra-left” groups for the violence, which erupted six months before the French go to the polls to elect Macron’s successor.
Interior minister Laurent Nunez said thousands of “far-left” protesters had been joined by “criminals who looted and ransacked” buildings across France.
A dispatch here from Sam Jones, our reporter in Madrid, as protests have spread to Italy and Portugal
The angry protests that have convulsed Spain and France in recent weeks have spilled over to Italy and Portugal , with rioters clashing with police and setting property on fire in Milan, and a tent encampment springing up in Lisbon over the weekend.
A march in central Milan on Saturday to protest against rising living costs began peacefully but ended with masked rioters throwing stones, paving blocks and other objects at riot police and setting fire to barricades made from bar tables.
Police used water cannon and teargas to disperse the crowds, and images of the aftermath showed a severely damaged carabinieri car.
At least two police officers were injured and about 50 demonstrators, including many minors, were detained, the LaPresse news agency reported.
Italy’s prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, said that while demonstrating was a right, “setting our cities ablaze is not”. In a social media post, she said “hooligans” had exploited the protests “to sow chaos, attack those responsible for ensuring security and to hold entire cities hostage”.
‘We are suffocating’: protests spread to Lisbon and Milan as housing and living cost tensions intensify
Emmanuel Macron will give a televised address to the French public this evening on the protests and unrest on Saturday.
The French President will speak at 8pm French time (6pm GMT), after more than 1,800 people were arrested on Saturday in connection with violence that spread from protests against the cost of living.
Paris police said about 110,000 people took part in a protest march on Saturday against the cost of living and school conditions.
Numbers have differed for those nationwide, with authorities saying it was about 550,000 but organisers claiming it was higher at about 800,000.
One person died of a heart attack, Paris police said. French media reported a protester suffered a medical emergency in the street during the march.
Thirteen police and gendarmerie officers and two firefighters were injured, the statement said, according to Associated Press.
The mayors of France’s three largest cities, Paris, Marseille and Lyon have requested a meeting with the prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, in the coming days.
Around Paris’ Place de la République on Sunday morning, dislodged cobblestones, shattered storefronts and broken glass marked the aftermath of the events.
Looting and damage were reported around the square and in some other tourist and shopping areas in the city centre.
Police said groups numbering from several hundred to more than 1,000 people formed unauthorised marches across central Paris on Saturday.
“By late afternoon, a new phase began with the arrival of large numbers of people whose sole aim was to steal and loot, taking advantage of the unrest,” police said.
Protests in France caused damage worth hundreds of millions of euros, according to the head of a trade body representing shop owners.
About 1,500 shops and retailers were damaged in the demonstrations according to Alexandre Bompard, president of the Retail and Trade Federation.
He told LCI television the cost to the establishments will run to “several hundreds of millions of euros”.
More than 1,800 people have been arrested in France over protests on Saturday, the country’s interior minister Laurent Nunez has said.
Nunez, in a post on X, said “the Republic will not yield” as more than 500 police officers, gendarmes and firefighters have been injured in the demonstrations.
“The material damage is considerable,” Nunez added, pointing to damaged shops.
He blamed thousands of “far-left” protesters along with “criminals who looted and ransacked” buildings across France.
“The Republic will yield nothing to those who seek to impose disorder and violence,” he said.
Causing disorder through violence and in a coordinated manner is not.
Attacking our law enforcement officers, targeting our institutions, damaging public buildings, breaking into prefectures or town halls, and looting businesses – none of this can be justified.
Following the events of 17 October – which, in some cities, continued late into the night-I wish to express my sincere gratitude and full support to the police officers, gendarmes, and firefighters who intervened under extreme conditions all across France.
By midday – and as early as the morning in Marseille – thousands of far-left individuals, intent on attacking public buildings and confronting our law enforcement, began committing acts of violence.
They were subsequently joined by criminals who looted and ransacked numerous businesses in several French cities, including Paris, Marseille, Lyon, Bordeaux, Rennes, Strasbourg, Grenoble, Nice, Limoges, and many others.
As of now, 1,800 people have been arrested, and investigations are already under way to identify the perpetrators so that they may be held accountable before the justice system.
At this stage, more than 500 police officers, gendarmes, and firefighters have been injured amid this violence.
Sadly, this casualty count is only provisional. The material damage is substantial, affecting, among others, hundreds of business owners.
The Republic will not yield to those who seek to impose disorder and violence.
It’s important to note that protests have also been taking place across Europe .
In Italy rioters clashed with police, looted stores and set property on fire in central Milan on Saturday.
The demonstration escalated after a march against wars and rising living costs began peacefully.
However masked protesters threw stones, paving blocks and other objects at riot police and set fire to barricades made from bar tables. Images of the aftermath showed a severely damaged carabinieri car.
Police used water cannons and teargas to disperse the crowds.
At least two police officers were injured and about 50 demonstrators, including many minors, were detained, the LaPresse news agency reported.
Meanwhile more peaceful protests took place in Portugal , with activists making calls for action to stop rising housing and living costs.
Hundreds of people gathered at Rossio Square in its capital, Lisbon, after a march that had seen thousands take to the streets across the country.
Reports from Agence France-Presse said the group in Lisbon vowed to stay overnight as they gathered around a statue of King Pedro IV in the square.
“The Portuguese social class that pays taxes, that which keeps this country going, is under attack and is losing its rights, notably its right to housing,” said Elena Costa, a 46-year-old social assistant.
Here’s a selection of photographs from the protests on Saturday and their aftermath, including the City Hall in Limoges.
The prefect on Sunday said the blaze in the 143-year-old building had been contained.

Photograph: Sylvain Thomas/AFP/Getty Images In case you are still catching up with the news from yesterday, my colleagues Kim Willsher and William Christou have this report.
More than 1,200 people were arrested in France on Saturday after protesters supporting high school students clashed with police, with some demonstrations later spiralling out of control as buildings were set ablaze and shops looted.
Police fired teargas in confrontations with protesters, as demonstrations across France were boosted by other groups angry about high prices and the fraying of a social welfare system. While hundreds of thousands protested peacefully in street marches in scores of cities, violent fringe groups targeted public buildings, luxury boutiques and supermarkets and attacked police vehicles and officers.
Late on Saturday, prime minister Sébastien Lecornu said 1,200 people had been arrested and 150 police hurt.
Interior minister Laurent Nuñez said the official demonstration had been hijacked by casseurs – “ opportunistic delinquents who had seen a chance to pillage and loot … we will find them and deal with them firmly”.
Buildings set ablaze and more than 1,200 arrested as police clash with protesters across France
Police in Paris arrested a “record figure” of 855 people during the protests on Saturday.
Agence France-Presse reported the number detained was the highest ever for a single event.
The figure forms part of the 1,200 arrested across France, as prime minister Sébastien Lecornu said 150 police had been hurt in clashes.
Meanwhile Deputy Mayor of Paris Lamia El Aaraje said the capital had been hit by “a level of violence that I believe we had never seen before”.
France is recovering after its worst protests in years saw buildings attacked and set ablaze across the country.
More than 1,200 people were arrested in the demonstrations on Saturday, which began with protests from students over the cost of living.
However violent fringe groups came out in support of the students, which saw events spiralling out of control.
Whole streets in Paris “have been devastated”, the city’s mayor, Emmanuel Gregoire, said.
Meanwhile in Limoges, central France, the town hall was “largely lost” to a fire set by masked protesters, the top regional official told the AFP news agency.
Authorities in France are now waiting to see if protests will go into another day. The protests began last month at schools ⁠in the poor northern suburbs of Paris , where ⁠anger over teacher ​absences and shabby facilities quickly morphed into a nationwide movement against inequality, weak public spending and falling standards.
We will be following events in France and bringing you any reaction as it comes in.

Oil prices over $100 could affect war with Iran, leading to escalation before elections - analysis
The US and Israel know that the main hurdle to keeping the lid on the war with Iran is the price of oil, and it will keep rising if no solution can be found for Hormuz and the Houthis.
Vessels transit the Strait of Hormuz off the coast of the port city of Bandar Abbas in southern Iran on September 5, 2026; illustrative
( photo credit : ATTA KENARE / AFP via Getty Images )
High oil prices are going to be an issue over the next few weeks if they continue to stay above $100 a barrel. That is a clear challenge for the United States and also potentially for Israel in terms of keeping a lid on a renewed conflict with Iran prior to the elections in both countries.
It is no secret that the looming elections have tended to change dynamics, estimations, and assessments about whether the conflict could start again.
The high oil prices come during a decline in stock prices on Wall Street. This is amid concerns about AI companies and energy prices. That could tend to be a kind of triple threat affecting the US, and thus also affecting Israel.
There has been a lot of messaging about how the Strait of Hormuz is open and the availability of alternative energy sources, but the question is whether or not the global market will accept these assertions.
Recent videos show ships sinking in the Strait of Hormuz and all sorts of containers floating away as ships are in distress. This is not something that will boost global optimism regarding supply chains, and it always remains a question whether enough ships are transporting energy supplies.
Flames burn at a facility belonging to Saudi oil giant Aramco south of Riyadh on October 3, 2026. (credit: AFP VIA GETTY IMAGES)
It also leads to questions about what the Houthis might do. The Houthis could try to threaten the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. They could also encourage other Iranian proxies, such as those in Iraq, to continue attacks on Saudi oil and gas energy infrastructure.
A mysterious explosion in Iraq on Saturday appears to have struck an Iranian proxy group. All this could continue to disrupt global trade.
When there are attacks on pipelines or transit points in Saudi Arabia, for instance, it takes weeks to repair them. That creates disruption, and all those disruptions add up to the feeling in the global market that there is too much uncertainty.
This kind of uncertainty will affect the US. It already appears to be affecting US policy regarding the Ukraine war and Russia, and this is the kind of thing that can lead to escalation in the Middle East or miscalculations in which something happens again with Iran.
Iran continues to be blockaded , but it also tends to feel a bit confident about its next steps. Therefore, we are seeing a potential for escalation within the next week or two.
Iran also knows there are elections in Israel and the US; therefore, Iran and its proxies may want to take advantage of this period.

Brent crude hovers near $109 a barrel as Ukraine resumes energy strikes, tankers attacked in Middle East
Smoke rises above the city following an air attack on the oil terminal in Saint Petersburg on October 18, 2026, amid the ongoing Russian-Ukrainian conflict.
Crude oil prices hovered near recent highs on Sunday as traders weighed a Ukraine bombing of oil facilities in Russia and more tankers coming under attack in the Persian Gulf.
Brent crude futures, the international benchmark, shed $1.04 to $108.82 per barrel. U.S. West Texas intermediate lost 26 cents to $101.15 per barrel.
Fires broke out at an oil terminal and depot in St. Petersburg after Ukraine launched a massive wave of drone strikes on Sunday, St. Petersburg Gov. Alexander Beglov said in a post on Telegram.
The terminal in St. Petersburg exports about 120,000 barrels per day of refined products, mostly fuel oil, according to data from Kpler. It is unclear how bad the damage is at the facility.
Ukraine briefly paused strikes on Russian energy facilities after President Donald Trump declared on Oct. 11 that Kyiv and Moscow had agreed to a truce .
Heavy smoke billows after Ukrainian drones hit infrastructure, according to local authorities, in St Petersburg, Russia June 3, 2026.
But Russia continued to strike Ukrainian energy infrastructure after Trump's announcement. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said last week that Kyiv would resume strikes on Russian facilities in retaliation.
In the Middle East, meanwhile, two tankers were attacked off the coast of Saudi Arabia in the Persian Gulf on Friday, according to incident reports from the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre.
A small boat fired a rocket-propelled grenade at an unidentified tanker 78 nautical miles northeast of Al Jubayl, according to UKMTO. Another tanker, the ST3, was hit by an unknown projectile, UKMTO reported.
Iran has escalated attacks on tankers in the Persian Gulf, Strait of Hormuz and Gulf of Oman in an effort to choke off crude oil exports from the region.

items.title: ‘Hybrid warfare’: Taiwan drives away 16 Chinese ships
items.summary: China is ramping up its presence around Taiwan, in a pattern that Taipei said is designed to 'alter the status quo'.
items.content:
Share ‘Hybrid warfare’: Taiwan drives away 16 Chinese ships on social media
Taiwan's coastguard said it took 'forceful action' to confront Chinese vessels [File: Cheng-chia Huang/AFP]
Taiwan has confronted and driven away 16 Chinese coastguard, research and fishing vessels that it said were involved in simultaneous “maritime harassment” operations.
An “unusually large” number of Chinese vessels took part in coordinated operations around Taiwan’s main island and Pratas (also known as Dongsha), a disputed island to the southwest, the Taiwanese coastguard said in a statement on Sunday.
